chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Salih ibn Abi Hammad, from al-Husayn ibn Yazid, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Ibrahim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, caused Adam and his wife to eat of the wheat, He expelled them both from Paradise and caused them to descend to the earth. Adam descended upon al-Safa and Hawwa descended upon al-Marwa. Al-Safa was named thus because it was derived from the name of Adam al-Mustafa (the Chosen), corresponding to the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'Surely Allah chose Adam and Noah.' And al-Marwa was named Marwa because it was derived from the name al-Mar'a (the woman).

Adam said: 'Nothing separated me from her except that she is not permissible for me. Had she been permissible for me, she would have descended with me upon al-Safa, but she was forbidden to me because of that, and separation was effected between me and her.'

Adam remained isolated from Hawwa. He would visit her during the day, conversing with her upon al-Marwa. But when night came and he feared being overcome by his desires, he would return to al-Safa and sleep there. Adam had no comfort except her, and for that reason women were called 'nisa'', because Hawwa was the 'uns' (companionship/comfort) for Adam.

Allah neither spoke to him nor sent him a messenger. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed upon him repentance and conveyed to him certain words. When he spoke these words, Allah turned towards him in mercy and sent Jibraeel (peace be upon him) to him. He said: 'Peace be upon you, O Adam, you who repent from your error and are patient through your tribulation. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent me to you to teach you the rites through which you can be purified.'

He took him by his hand and led him to the place of the House (Ka'ba). Allah sent down upon him a cloud that shaded the place of the House, and the cloud was aligned with the Bayt al-Ma'mur (the Frequented House above). He said: 'O Adam, mark with your foot the area where this cloud has shaded you, for a house of white gem will be brought forth for you, becoming your qibla and the qibla of your offspring after you.' Adam (peace be upon him) did so, and Allah brought forth beneath the cloud a house of white gem. And Allah sent down the Black Stone, which was whiter than milk and more radiant than the sun; it turned black only because the polytheists wiped themselves with it — from the filth of the polytheists the Stone turned black. Jibraeel (peace be upon him) commanded him to seek Allah's forgiveness from his sin at all the sacred sites, and informed him that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had forgiven him, and instructed him to carry pebbles for the jamarat from al-Muzdalifa.

When he reached the place of the jamarat, Iblees confronted him and said: 'O Adam, where are you headed?' Jibraeel (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Do not speak to him; pelt him with seven pebbles and proclaim the takbir with each pebble.' So Adam (peace be upon him) did so until he had finished pelting the stones.

He commanded him to offer the sacrifice — that is, the hady (sacrificial animal) — before pelting the jamarat. And he commanded him to shave his head in humility before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So Adam did that. Then he commanded him to visit the House and circumambulate it seven times, and to hasten between al-Safa and al-Marwa seven times, beginning at al-Safa and ending at al-Marwa.

Then he commanded him to visit the House, to circumambulate it seven times, and to walk briskly between Al-Safa and Al-Marwa seven times, beginning at Al-Safa and ending at Al-Marwa. Then after that, he circumambulated seven more times around the House — this is the Tawaf al-Nisa'. It is not permissible for the one in ihram to approach his wife until he performs the Tawaf al-Nisa'. Adam (peace be upon him) did so.

Then Jibraeel said to him: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forgiven your sin, accepted your repentance, and made your wife permissible to you.' So Adam went forth, and his sin was forgiven, his repentance was accepted, and his wife was made permissible to him.

key_terms.الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةِ: Al-Safa and al-Marwa — the two hills in Mecca between which sa'y is performed
key_terms.الْبَيْتُ الْمَعْمُورُ: Bayt al-Ma'mur — the Frequented House in the heavens, the celestial counterpart to the Ka'ba
key_terms.الْجِمَارُ: The jamarat — the stone pillars representing Iblees, pelted during hajj
key_terms.الْحَجَرُ الْأَسْوَدُ: The Black Stone — originally white, turned black from polytheists' contact
key_terms.الْحِنْطَةَ: The wheat — the forbidden fruit Adam and Hawwa ate in Paradise
key_terms.الْمَنَاسِكُ: The hajj rites/rituals taught by Jibraeel to Adam
key_terms.الْمَهَاة: White gem (onyx/crystal) — the material from which the first Ka'ba was built
key_terms.الْمُزْدَلِفَةُ: Muzdalifa — the sacred plain where hajj pilgrims spend the night and collect pebbles
key_terms.الْمُصْطَفَى: Al-Mustafa — the Chosen One, an epithet of Adam (and later the Prophet Muhammad)
key_terms.طَوَافُ النِّسَاءِ: Tawaf al-nisa' — the circumambulation that makes one's spouse permissible again after ihram

ai.seo_question: What is the origin of the hajj rituals according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), narrating through Imam al-Kadhim (peace be upon him), recounts the origin narrative of hajj: after Adam and Hawwa were expelled from Paradise for eating the wheat, they descended separately — Adam on al-Safa and Hawwa on al-Marwa — and remained separated during a period of divine silence. The Imam explains the etymological origins of the names 'Safa' (from al-Mustafa, the Chosen) and 'Marwa' (from al-Mar'a, the woman), and 'nisa'' (women, from 'uns', companionship). Upon Adam's repentance, Angel Jibraeel taught him the complete hajj rituals — including tawaf, sa'y, the Ka'ba's establishment, the Black Stone's descent, stoning of Iblees at the jamarat, sacrifice, shaving, and tawaf al-nisa' — by which his sin was expiated and his wife was restored to him. This narrative provides the theological foundation for hajj as an act of purification, rooted in Adam's original sin and repentance.
